feed.title: Re: Safer sighashes and more granular SIGHASH_NOINPUT

entry.title: Re: Safer sighashes and more granular SIGHASH_NOINPUT
entry.summary:
The role of OP_CODESEPARATOR in Taproot scripts is under scrutiny due to changes in how conditional logic is handled within Bitcoin’s scripting system. Traditionally, OP_CODESEPARATOR enabled selective signing of certain script fragments, particularly useful alongside conditional opcodes like OP_IF. With the advent of merklized scripts in Taproot, much of the functionality previously reliant on conditionals has shifted, raising questions about the ongoing relevance of OP_CODESEPARATOR.
If OP_CODESEPARATOR no longer serves a practical purpose, its removal could streamline validation code and simplify implementation. However, if it retains value in specific scenarios, such as when paired with NOINPUT, efforts should be made to ensure compatibility. The commitment of H(masked_script) adds clarity to the position and function of CODESEPARATOR, but without this commitment, reliance falls on the assumption that a public key is exclusively used within a given script template, which may not always hold true.
Beyond the specifics of OP_CODESEPARATOR, script masking does not address vulnerabilities associated with address or scriptPubKey reuse—an especially prevalent type of reuse within the network. Nevertheless, masking does offer protection against replayability in cases where the same public key appears across different scripts, mitigating certain classes of attacks even if it does not solve all issues related to script reuse.
